title: CASE OF DZELADINOV AND OTHERS v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
conclusion: No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Procedural aspect)
summary:
In the case of Dzeladinov and Others v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicants, all members of the Roma community, brought a complaint against the state following a violent incident involving police intervention. The case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Travellers to police violence and the lack of effective protection or redress when abuses occur, particularly in situations marked by ethnic tension and social exclusion. On the night of 2 August 1998, after a Roma circumcision celebration in Štip, a fight broke out involving a police-affiliated individual. Police officers responded by entering the restaurant and, according to the applicants, assaulted numerous Roma guests, including a pregnant woman who was denied immediate medical care. Several applicants were allegedly beaten, insulted on account of their ethnic origin, and detained for hours, with some forced to confess under duress. Despite photographic evidence of injuries, the authorities failed to conduct a thorough investigation into the applicants’ complaints.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Article 3 of the Convention, which prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. While the Court found no substantive violation of Article 3 regarding the alleged ill-treatment itself, it held that there had been a procedural violation due to the authorities’ failure to effectively investigate the applicants’ credible allegations. This judgment is significant as it underscores the persistent challenges Roma and Travellers face in securing justice and accountability for police misconduct, reflecting broader historical patterns of marginalisation and impunity in Europe.
